utterances.text: Yes. Dr. Turkusic, that concludes your testimony. Thank you for your coming to the Tribunal to give it, on behalf of the Bench and the Tribunal as well. Now you're free to go.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Thank you, Your Honours. Fiat iustitia et pereat mundus.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: As I indicated, we will adjourn for a month from now, and then when we will have heard from the Prosecution, Mr. Tieger, that -- as to the witnesses we have to hear because of several logistical problems, we will let the parties know when we will resume. But there is one matter I want to raise at -- today. This concerns the

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, I mentioned during the course of yesterday's hearing that I would come back to the issue of your cross-examination. As you are aware, in June of this year, the Chamber determined that it was necessary in the interest of fair and expeditious trial and for reasons of trial management to impose reasonable time limits on your cross-examination. The Chamber does not approach the assessment of what constitutes a reasonable time in each instance arbitrarily. Quite to the contrary, as I have noted before, the Chamber considers a range of factors, including your estimate of time you will require, the scope of the anticipated testimony, the type of witness, the quantity and type of written evidence proffered by the Prosecution for the witness, the number and nature of associate exhibits tendered for that witness, and the length of testimony and cross-examination in the previous case or cases that the witness testified in. As Judge Morrison mentioned yesterday, taking into account that you are not a lawyer trained and experienced in cross-examination, to date we have given you considerable leeway in conducting your cross-examination, including by -- in almost every instance extending the time we considered reasonable, often multiple times. However, granting you additional time has not resulted in you conducting your cross-examination efficiently, focusing your cross-examination on matters relevant to the case which the witness is in a position to comment on or desisting from reading at length from documents and making unnecessary commentary. You regularly complain that you do not have enough time to cover issues you consider to be important with the witnesses. The problem is not the time limit that has been given to you. It is, rather, that you waste a lot of time in the conduct of your cross-examination. The Chamber has offered you advice on multiple occasions on how to improve, and we strongly suggest once again that you also get and pay heed to advice from your legal advisors. The Chamber expects you to comply with the time limits that we set for your cross-examination of each witness. To that end, you must prepare your cross-examination to ensure that you will be completed at the end of the time allocated to you. We will no longer be extending the time for your cross-examination as a general rule. We also note at this stage your ability to cross-examine is central to whether you are adequately representing yourself, and has therefore fair trial implications. It is your job to ensure that you address the issues relevant to your case in your cross-examination. If you continue to show that you are unable to conduct your cross-examination properly and within a reasonable time, so much so that fair trial is affected to the extent that you cannot cover important and relevant issues despite the sufficient time allowed to you, the Chamber may find that to be grounds for limiting your right to self-representation and requiring that one of your legal advisors, or indeed Mr. Harvey, take over the task of cross-examination. There is one further matter I would like to raise, that of translations of documents being used during your cross-examination, as raised by Mr. Tieger. The absence of translation into English of documents put to the witness by you, Mr. Karadzic, has been a cause of concern by the Chamber for some time. The lack of translation makes it difficult for those in the courtroom to follow your line of questioning and slows down considerably your cross-examination of witnesses. It also creates a lot of work for your team and the Chamber's staff outside the courtroom, as determination of admissibility of each untranslated document that has been MFI'd have to be made at a later stage. It is up to you and your team to ensure that if you want to put a document to a witness, you have a translation of that document. We've said that before and have seen no discernible improvement on this. If the situation does not improve from this point on, we will consider preventing you from putting untranslated documents to witnesses at all. Once again, I emphasise that it is your task as lead counsel in your own defence to organise your team and your -- and considerable resources that have been put at your disposal properly. The inability to do so may also factor into any decision by the Chamber to limit your right to self-representation. I therefore urge you to work closely together in the pro se office and the CLSS to manage the translation process more efficiently. Unless there's anything to be raised by the parties -- yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to respond, with your leave, briefly, on both issues. First of all, as regards examination, I greatly appreciate and owe great thanks to the Trial Chamber for their understanding both due to my inexperience as a lawyer and lack of experience in cross-examination for which they had understanding, but it was quite recently that Honourable Judge Morrison told me that the Trial Chamber would not take into account peripheral matters. Witnesses speak at length about all sorts of things here. They make assertions about political and factual matters that need to be responded to, and we have to be sure that they will be rejected, not taken into account. Second, the OTP has the ambition to overload this case with a huge number of documents and a huge number of claims by witnesses. With due respect to this Trial Chamber, I must say that in other judgements I have seen, the Trial Chambers give credit to peripheral elements, while at the same time rejecting reports by United Nations or observers, et cetera. So I have great reasons for concern without pre-empting what this Trial Chamber would do in this case. But if a single claim can determine something in the judgement, then the Defence has to deal with that claim. I have to tell you that regardless of the fact that I will have problems with time restrictions, I will not assign to anyone else the right to lead my defence, and I will have to fight for my right to self-representation by all means. Not because I have no confidence in Mr. Harvey or his team, but because nobody knows the facts as I know them. Therefore, nobody can defend me. I have seen innocent people being convicted because their very good lawyers were unable to know the facts. As far as translations are concerned --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, I note the time. It's time to rise, and I don't feel the need to respond each item you raised. All I can say at this moment is that take seriously what I have told you today. We'll rise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: at 12.16 p.m. sine die
